tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'24 paper compares SIEVE against LRU (Cachelib's optimized LRU for throughput) plus FIFO, ARC and 7 other policies for miss ratio. The code is public (cacheMon/NSDI24-SIEVE simulator snapshot; Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23 prototype) and the CPU model is stated (c6420, Intel Gold 6142 @ 2.6 GHz, turbo off, one NUMA node), but the compiler and flags are not, so it cannot be A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Cachelib-based prototype: SIEVE is 16% faster than Cachelib's optimized LRU (17% vs TwoQ) at 1 thread on both the Meta and Twitter KV traces. At 16 threads it has more than 2x the throughput of optimized LRU and TwoQ on the Meta trace (the contributions list says 125% higher than optimized LRU). Optimized LRU itself scales about 6x from 1 to 16 threads on Twitter; only the unoptimized LRU plateaus at 4 threads. Miss ratio in libCacheSim: on CDN1 at the large cache size, SIEVE reduces FIFO's miss ratio by a mean of 21%, and by more than 42% on 10% of traces (p90 whisker). Over 1559 traces it reduces ARC's miss ratio by up to 63.2% (mean 1.5%). The paper frames that 1.5% mean as significant next to ARC's own mean 6.3% reduction over LRU; the 1.5% is smaller than the 6.3%, not larger.
corrections.workload: 1559 traces from 7 datasets (247,017 million requests, 14,852 million objects; Twitter, Meta, Wikimedia, TencentPhoto and two proprietary CDNs) replayed in libCacheSim for miss ratio. Separately, a Cachelib (C++) prototype replays two production KV traces (Meta, Twitter) with 1-16 threads, with cache size 4 x nthreads GB, to measure throughput.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 347 stars (libCacheSim); sievecache.com (redirects to cachemon.github.io/SIEVE-website) lists adopters including Immudb, TiDB, Pelikan, DragonFly, DNSCrypt-proxy, PostgREST and Ceph
corrections.caveats: The paper states the CPU model, NUMA pinning and turbo-boost setting for the throughput prototype but not the compiler or optimization flags, so it is capped at tier B. The miss-ratio numbers come from the libCacheSim simulator. The throughput numbers come from a separate Cachelib-based C++ prototype (Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23), not from libCacheSim. The >2x throughput result at 16 threads is reported for the Meta trace only. The paper is internally inconsistent about ARC's mean reduction over LRU: the introduction says 6.7% (up to 33.7%) and Section 4.2 says 6.3%. libCacheSim's Sieve.c is a simulator policy, not a drop-in production cache.

notes: The original claim misattributed the 4-thread plateau to the optimized LRU; in the paper it applies only to the unoptimized LRU. The claim also inverted the 1.5% vs 6.3% comparison. The core >2x-at-16-threads and 63.2%-vs-ARC numbers are on the page. The metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 347 stars, not archived or a fork, last commit 2026-09-26 (active). The phrase 'production-ready' does not appear on sievecache.com; the site lists adopters, so stars_or_usage was reworded.

tier_reason: The TinyLFU paper (arXiv 1512.00727v2) plots hit ratio against LRU, ARC, LIRS and others, but those results come from the authors' Java simulator and Caffeine, not from this C++ port. The repo has no benchmark of its own, so it stays at C for this entry.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Per the paper (not this port), W-TinyLFU with a 1% window matched or beat every other evaluated policy on the majority of traces, including LRU, ARC and LIRS. It outperformed all other policies on DS1, SPC1-like and the search-engine traces. On OLTP, F1 and F2, the 1% window was not the top performer; a 20-40% window was needed. On P8/P12 it led at all but the largest cache sizes. The ~89% figure is TinyLFU's memory saving over a strawman sliding-window sketch (Zipf 0.9, 1K cache, 9K histogram), not a result against LRU.
corrections.caveats: The quantitative hit-ratio results come from the original paper's Java simulator and Caffeine evaluation. They were not re-measured on this C++11 header-only port, so the entry is tier C even though the algorithm's paper is well cited. The README says thread-safety and hash-collision protection are absent. The repo has no LICENSE file. Caffeine itself (the canonical TinyLFU implementation) is already catalogued and excluded.

notes: The claim 'best on every tested trace' is overstated: the paper's own OLTP/F1/F2 results show the default 1% window losing, and the abstract's 'equal or better' wording is qualified in Section 5. The metadata checks out: no license (gh license null, no LICENSE file in the root), 64 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2018-10-24 (abandoned). This is a small independent reimplementation.
